title: The call of the king
hook: a good king's call, heard first, and then Christ's

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first week: sin, then mercy, then a colloquy at the foot of the cross. Your line was what have I done for Christ. What came back when you asked it? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

A recruiting speech, and an unusual one. A king stands before his people and says: come with me. You'll eat what I eat, wear what I wear, work with me by day and keep watch with me by night. Share the hard part, and you'll share the victory. No promise of easy pay. Just: with me. Ignatius had been a soldier before his conversion, and this page of the Exercises sounds like it. He asks the person praying to hear that speech, and to notice how any decent person would answer it. Then he turns the page. Today: the call of the king.
screen: `COME WITH ME.` → `SAME FOOD, SAME WORK, SAME NIGHTS.` → `THEN HE TURNS THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: The call of the king stands at the doorway of the second week, and it works like a parable in two steps. First, a human king. Ignatius pictures a leader chosen by God, good and just, calling people in the terms of his own century to a hard campaign. The campaign isn't the point. The way he calls is. No orders from a safe distance. Same food, same clothes, same nights. Ignatius says it would be shameful to hear a call like that and hang back. Step two: if that's how we'd answer a good human leader, how much more Christ. Now the king is Christ our Lord, and the call goes out to every person. His aim, as Ignatius puts it, is to bring the whole world to his Father, and whoever wants to come must labor with him, so that following him in the pain, they may follow him in the glory. The Gospels have a shorter version of the same call. By the Sea of Galilee, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says to two fishermen: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men." No list of benefits. Just after me. Ignatius then notices two kinds of answer. Anyone with judgment and reason, he says, will offer themselves for the work. Some will want to go further and offer more: to follow even into poverty and insult, if that is what Christ chooses for them. The Exercises leave that further offering to the person's freedom. At work or at home, the meditation leaves a plain question about whoever is calling you: do they send you into the work, or walk into it first?
screen: `A KING WHO SHARES THE HARD PART.` · `HOW MUCH MORE CHRIST.` · `TWO KINDS OF ANSWER.` · `WHO WALKS INTO THE WORK FIRST?` · then, large: `COME YE AFTER ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer the call. Settle, and breathe. Hear it in its shortest form: come after me. If you pray, you can answer Christ in your own words, or simply with today's line, I want to follow. Then ask, quietly, where. Not the whole rest of your life. Just tomorrow. Let one place come to mind: a kitchen, a desk, a hospital corridor, a phone call you've been avoiding. If you don't pray, you can think of someone you'd follow because they worked right beside you, and ask what made the difference. The bell holds the time.
The call of the king. A good king's call, heard first, so that Christ's call can be heard more clearly. Today's word.
screen: `THE CALL OF THE KING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I want to follow. Today, notice one leader, at work, at home or on the news, who goes first into the hard part, and say the line once when you see it. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: In an Ignatian retreat, the meditation on the call of the king is prayed before the second week begins, as a way of asking how fully the person wants to follow Christ.

original.note: Greek of Matthew 4:19: come, after me. the call to the fishermen.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a medieval king.
what it means: a two-step meditation: notice how you'd answer a good human leader, then hear Christ's call.
what a scholar hears: it stands at the doorway of the second week, and the argument rests on one detail: this king shares his followers' food, clothes and labor.

sources.ref: Spiritual Exercises, the call of the temporal king (no. 91–98)
Autobiography of Ignatius of Loyola (his life as a soldier before his conversion)

notes: The human king's campaign in Ignatius's text is framed in the crusading language of his time (conquering the lands of unbelievers). The script deliberately says only 'a hard campaign, in the terms of his own century' so that no tradition is cast as the enemy. Confirm this is acceptable.

Paraphrases of nos. 91–98: 'following me in the pain, may follow me in the glory'; 'all who have judgment and reason will offer their entire selves to the work'; the further 'offering of greater value'. Confirm.
Index hook ('imagine a good king's call, then Christ's') is rephrased in the hook field to avoid the 'Imagine' opening; word and carry are kept exactly.
Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 4:19 and the Greek 'δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου' to confirm.
Editor: the repeated 'On a Tuesday' closer replaced.
